---
title: "Generating sigma-algebras"
---

The [closure requirements](event-spaces.qmd#closure-requirements) say that a
sigma-algebra must contain complements and countable unions. Suppose we want to
assign probabilities to the full three-way lemma distinction and the two-way
dependency-relation distinction. We thus seek the smallest sigma-algebra
generated by both partitions.

Recall that an [event](events.qmd) is a set of token outcomes. A generator names
events whose distinctions must remain visible; closure then supplies the other
events needed for coherent probability assignments.

We obtain that sigma-algebra from its atoms, compare it with coarser generators, and then ask when adding a generator creates no new measurable distinction.

For a collection $\mathcal C$ of subsets of $\Omega$,

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C)
$$

denotes the smallest sigma-algebra containing every set in $\mathcal C$. The collection $\mathcal C$ is a [**generating set**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces), and $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ is the sigma-algebra it generates.

```{r}
#| label: load-generators-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
wh$outcome_id <- paste(wh$split, wh$sentence_id, wh$token_id, sep = ":")

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L, !anyDuplicated(wh$outcome_id))

lemma_sets <- split(wh$outcome_id, wh$lemma)
relation_sets <- split(wh$outcome_id, wh$dependency_relation)
```

## Generators and atoms

Let $H$, $K$, and $N$ be the lemma events for *hangi*, *kim*, and *ne*, and let $S$ and $O$ be the relation events for `nsubj` and `obj`. The generating collection is

$$
\mathcal C
\equiv
\{H,K,N,S,O\}.
$$

Because the three lemma events partition $\Omega$ and the two relation events partition $\Omega$, the nonempty atoms are the intersections

$$
A_{\ell,r}
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)=\ell,\ R(\omega)=r\}.
$$

Before the six-atom construction, consider only $N$ and $O$. Their truth-value
combinations yield $N\cap O$, $N\cap O^c$, $N^c\cap O$, and
$N^c\cap O^c$. Every event that can be expressed using these generators is a
union of those four atoms, so the generated sigma-algebra has $2^4=16$ events.
The six-atom case below repeats the same construction with a finer lemma
partition.

```{r}
#| label: generate-finite-event-space
atoms <- split(
  wh$outcome_id,
  interaction(wh$lemma, wh$dependency_relation, sep = " × ", drop = TRUE)
)
atom_sizes <- data.frame(
  atom = names(atoms),
  tokens = lengths(atoms),
  row.names = NULL
)

all_unions <- unlist(
  lapply(
    0:length(atoms),
    function(k) combn(names(atoms), k, simplify = FALSE)
  ),
  recursive = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  all(atom_sizes$tokens > 0),
  sum(atom_sizes$tokens) == nrow(wh),
  length(all_unions) == 2^length(atoms)
)

c(nonempty_atoms = length(atoms), events = length(all_unions))
```

The empirical cross-classification yields `r length(atoms)` nonempty atoms. Their unions form `r length(all_unions)` events in $\sigma(\mathcal C)$. Each union is included because closure requires it, not because it corresponds to a familiar linguistic label.

```{r}
#| label: plot-generated-atoms
#| fig-cap: "Token counts in the lemma-by-relation atoms of the generated event space."
ggplot(atom_sizes, aes(reorder(atom, tokens), tokens)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65") +
  geom_point(color = "#2C7FB8", size = 2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tokens") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Coarser generators

A generator that records only whether the lemma is *ne* produces the two atoms $N$ and $N^c$. It cannot separate *hangi* from *kim*. Adding the object event refines those atoms into the four cells shown on the preceding page. Adding the three-way lemma partition refines the space again into the observed lemma-by-relation cells.

This gives a finite construction procedure:

1. list the distinctions supplied by the generators;
2. intersect each distinction with the others and their complements;
3. discard empty intersections;
4. take every union of the remaining atoms.

For a finite sample space, this procedure produces the smallest sigma-algebra containing the chosen generators.

“Smallest” rules out distinctions that the generators did not request. Empty
intersections are discarded because they contain no outcomes and cannot form a
new atom. In the code, `interaction()` names the nonempty cross-classified
atoms, `combn()` enumerates selections of atom names, and `unlist()` collects
all of their unions.

## When a generator adds no distinction

If $T$ is the certain event $\Omega$, then adding $T$ to the generating set splits no atom:

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C\cup\{\Omega\})
=
\sigma(\mathcal C).
$$

Likewise, adding an event already expressible as a union of the existing atoms does not enlarge the sigma-algebra. What matters is whether the new event divides at least one existing atom.

The generators retain only lemma and the two selected dependency relations.
Tokens with other interrogative lemmas or relations never enter these atoms, and
register was not used to split them. The resulting event space can therefore
answer probability questions about the represented lemma-by-relation cells, but
it contains no event whose mass measures omitted constructions or Turkish usage
outside the five source registers.

Generators determine the finest distinctions a probability measure can express. The [next page](probability-measures.qmd) assigns empirical mass to those distinctions.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `atoms` to identify the smallest atom and inspect its source rows in `wh`.
2. If the relation generator is removed, how many nonempty atoms remain in this dataset? Compute the number of unions they generate.
3. Show that the event “lemma is not *ne*” is already a union of two lemma atoms and thus adds no new distinction.
4. Why would a generator for register enlarge this event space? What dependence warning would then become relevant?
5. Why does adding a singleton token generator enlarge the space even though
   that token already belongs to one existing atom?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The smallest atom is the single *hangi*–`obj` token, `train:ins_1722:2`, whose surface form is *Hangisini*. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Removing the relation generator leaves three nonempty lemma atoms, and their unions form $2^3=8$ events. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The event ‘lemma is not *ne*’ is the union of the disjoint *hangi* and *kim* atoms, so it introduces no new distinction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A register generator would split any lemma–relation atom that occurs across registers; those register clusters would also warn against treating the retained rows as iid usage tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The singleton generator separates one outcome from the other outcomes in
   its current atom, creating a finer partition and thus new unions.

</details>

Generators induce atoms by intersection, and their smallest sigma-algebra
contains every union of those atoms without introducing additional
distinctions. Thus, adding a generator enlarges the event space only when it
splits an existing atom. The [next page](probability-measures.qmd) assigns mass
to these measurable unions.
